text:
I need an email to win back customers who cancelled. I own a home cleaning company with 18 cleaners.

What's true:
- We have 212 regular customers. 64 cancelled in the last year. In exit surveys, the most common reason was price, then a different cleaner showing up each time.
- An every-other-week cleaning for a 3-bedroom house costs $165 with us. The app services in our area charge about $140.
- Our cleaners are employees, not contractors. We pay $21 an hour and carry insurance on every visit.
- Last year 7 of our 18 cleaners left, so about 4 in 10 customers had their regular cleaner change at least once.
- We now give each customer a regular cleaner and a named backup.
- Returning customers get their first cleaning for $99.

I want the email to promise that you'll get the same cleaner every single time. Keep it to about 150 words.

Before I draft, one thing to settle: **the facts don't support "same cleaner every single time."** You give each customer a regular cleaner *and a named backup*, which means sometimes the backup comes. Last year 7 of 18 cleaners left. These are customers who left partly because their cleaner kept changing, so if the first sick day breaks a promise of "every single time," they'll leave again and won't come back a second time. What you can honestly promise is just as strong: "Your cleaner, by name. If they're ever out, it's your named backup, someone you've met, never a stranger." I'd write it that way unless you can guarantee it some other way (see question 2).

A few questions that would change the email:

1. **The $99 offer:** Is there a deadline or catch, like having to rebook every other week, a minimum number of visits, or a size limit? What does a cleaning cost after the first one: $165 again, or a returning-customer rate?
2. **Keeping cleaners:** Has anything changed that should keep your cleaners from leaving, like a raise, benefits, or better scheduling? Any number on turnover this year so far? This is what makes the "your cleaner" promise believable.
3. **What happens if you miss:** If a stranger shows up anyway, or the clean isn't right, what do you do? A free re-clean, a refund, the next visit free?
4. **Price vs. the apps:** Are you OK naming the roughly $25 gap and explaining it (employees paid $21/hr, insured on every visit, same person in your home)? Or would you rather not mention the apps?
5. **From and to:** Who signs it, you by name? Can it use the customer's first name and their old cleaner's name, if that cleaner is still with you?
6. **Anything they'll find out anyway:** Did any price change, policy change or bad incident come up in the exit surveys or reviews that this email should face head-on?

Answer whichever you can. For anything you don't know, I'll write around it rather than guess.

OK, you're right, I can't promise every single time because of sick days and holidays. Go with the named backup wording, as strong as you can make it.

1. Offer ends December 31. No catch that I know of. After that I don't know, I'd assume $165, but I can't match $140.
2. Since we started regular cleaners in July, 1 of our 18 cleaners has left. I don't know about raises or benefits beyond the $21/hr.
3. I don't know.
4. Yes, name it. The app services mostly use contractors with no insurance on the visit.
5. Me, Lisa Grant, owner of Brightway Home Cleaning. I don't know about using first names or old cleaner names.
6. Not that I know of. Also: no contract, they can cancel any time. They book by replying to the email or calling 555-0164.

I've written it to the true version of the promise: your cleaner every time, and when they can't come, a backup you already know by name.

<final_document>
Subject: You told us why you left. We fixed it.

Hi,

When you cancelled, you gave us two reasons: price, and a different cleaner showing up too often. You were right about the cleaners. Last year 7 of our 18 left, and too many of you opened the door to a stranger.

Since July, every customer has a regular cleaner and a named backup. When your cleaner is sick or on holiday, your backup comes. You'll always know who's coming. Since we made this change, 1 of our 18 cleaners has left.

On price: we charge $165 for an every-other-week clean of a 3-bedroom home, and app services nearby charge about $140. The difference pays for cleaners who are employees earning $21 an hour, with insurance on every visit. Most app services use contractors, with no insurance on the visit.

Come back and your first cleaning is $99, through December 31. There's no contract, and you can cancel any time.

Reply to this email or call 555-0164.

Lisa Grant
Owner, Brightway Home Cleaning
</final_document>

Some notes:

- **It's about 170 words.** To get to 150, cut the last sentence of the price paragraph, about app contractors. That makes the email a little weaker, though, because that sentence is your best answer to the price objection.
- **Price after the $99 visit:** The email states $165 as your current rate. It doesn't promise what visits after the first will cost, because you weren't sure. If $165 is definitely the price after the first visit, you could add "then $165 after that" to the offer line. These readers left over price, so it's better they hear it from you than on their first bill.
- **Things I left out because you didn't know them:** what happens if a stranger shows up anyway, and personal details like first names and old cleaners' names. If you decide on a make-good, for example "if anyone other than your cleaner or backup shows up, that visit is free," add it after "You'll always know who's coming." It would make the promise much stronger. Also, if a customer's old cleaner still works for you, "Maria is still with us" would probably do more than anything else in the email.
